{
  "question_intent": "Bank of America's capital strategy and US card business outlook",
  "main_topics": ["capital strategy", "US card business", "regulatory impact", "retail market growth", "customer repayment rates"],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "High",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": true,
  "contains_forward_guidance": false,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "question_quote": "Can I take you back on capital? So, I guess there's now a little bit of a divergence in terms of you know some of your peers saying they're going to go down 13%, and others being very clear that they're comfortable with the full range. So the upper end of the range is the guidance. I understand that some of that is to do with general uncertainty, and some of that is to do with the timing of the regulatory change. But even then, the [Maximum Distributable Amount hurdle] move was only about 20 basis points. So just wondering how you're thinking about that. On the call a few weeks ago, you also said that it is not inconceivable that sitting at [13.9%], in the next couple of quarters we might go through that range. So would you stay there, or would you always pay back to the top end of the range as it were? So that's number one and number two is on US cards. So I guess maybe the dust has settled a little bit since liberation day in terms of consumer behaviour, what have you seen? I guess the question is less about asset quality, but more that in the past, certainly the full year, there was some guidance and ambition about growing more in the retail segment of the consumer market. Is that still where you're comfortable going? Is that where consumers want to spend? Thank you.",
  "answer_quote": "Okay, thank you Perlie. So at the full year, what we said was you should expect us to operate towards the upper half of our target range of 13 to 14%. The reason we said that was really two things. Firstly, it was the Pillar 2A impact of IRB, but it was also the fact that some of the reductions that we might have anticipated in Pillar 2 are now further out, because the implementation of Basel is further out. But we also said that would leave our distribution plans unaffected. So you should take from that that we'd always plan to be in that kind of zone. We were just being clearer with you with that disclosure. In terms of where we are now, I would distinguish how and why? So how are we there? We're there because that is what the strategy is designed to do. The strategy is designed to create higher, more consistent levels of returns, that will in turn generate higher levels of capital. So we shouldn't be surprised by the capital trajectory in the firm. That is the modus operandi of the plan. So now we find ourselves here, what does that mean? We are clearly reflecting the uncertainty in the economic environment, we're very mindful of that. And as we make decisions about how to deploy our capital, we are still very mindful of the hierarchy that we gave you, that remains intact. So it's number one, ensuring that we are robust from a regulatory perspective. Number two, delivering our distribution plans, which is at least £10 billion over the three years and number three, investing in our businesses. So from our perspective, the outcome and what we see now is very much in line with what we originally planned. It's conceivable that we go through the top end of our range, but again, that would be in the context of the plans that we set out for you and the priorities that we've given. So I wouldn't add any more than that. In terms of US cards, our book is biased, if you like, towards super prime. That is a great position from a credit perspective, but actually leaves us with some opportunities as a risk adjusted margin matter. You should expect us to continue to seek out retail partners as we have done in the past. That is a long term strategic goal, to rebalance this portfolio away from the concentration that it currently has in travel. Clearly, we'll be very thoughtful about that, but that strategy remains intact. And we do look at risk adjusted margins, that's really important to us and we believe that by doing so, the risk adjusted margin of this book will continue to increase, that's our opportunity. In terms of customer behaviour, no significant change, only what we called out, I think, for a couple of quarters now, which is customers continue to repay at very high levels. So if you look at customer repayment rates [on slide] 38. If you look at the customer repayment rates, they're at 32%, which is significantly elevated still versus the pre COVID position, even after all of the credit normalisation in the US. So if it's having any effect at all, it's probably having a bit of a drag effect on the ability to build balances, but we're happy with that balance at this point in time."
}
